name: Colin Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the team that builds inventory software for a tech company, and I have a master’s degree. Most mornings I review overnight stock errors from retail shops and use AI to draft a test before I talk to whoever was on call. I like solving a real shop problem quickly, but the night phone can swallow a whole weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI saves me the boring first pass on tests, while our inventory software still needs someone to answer when a warehouse count is wrong. I use it every day, but I read the change before it goes live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m paid the usual senior developer wage, and I have about three months of basic bills saved. The company has several retail customers, so a small AI gain seems more like another tool than an immediate threat to my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading the inventory team and put 150 a month into savings while wages hold. In the first year, I’d keep checking every AI-written change against a real stock count before a release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel mostly calm about work. The on-call phone is still tiring, but this picture does not make the roster look smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does an on-call mistake look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a shop showed twelve coats it did not have, and the night supervisor rang me. A wrong stock count can ring my phone before breakfast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does three months saved feel enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It covers a short gap, not a long search. I add to it because I want more freedom to say no to a bad contract someday.

say: I say **AI tests** save a first pass, while people still answer for stock errors.
I tell my team to **read changes** before they go live.
think: I see **steady retail customers** and ordinary pay as fairly secure for now.
I know **three months saved** would not cover a long job search.
do: **Keep leading** the inventory team and review AI-written changes against real stock counts.
feel: **Mostly calm** about work, despite tiring on-call shifts.
S0.quote: A wrong stock count can ring my phone before breakfast.
fieldNote: Daily AI use sits inside his **human release check**, not an automatic approval.
His **three-month cushion** and several customers support confidence, while on-call work still tires him.

steps.text: Keep leading inventory releases and compare AI changes against stock counts
Save 150 monthly while senior developer pay continues

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell coworkers the company should share the productivity gain instead of quietly cutting entry-level jobs. I’d join the workplace group asking for paid AI training and clear limits on night calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this already looks possible: software now drafts code and checks it faster than a new developer. I could lead a smaller crew, but I might lose overtime pay if the company uses the savings to cut coverage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d learn a new AI method for tracing stock errors across stores and compare it with our incident log. In the first year of strong change, I’d join the workplace group’s talks on staffing and on-call pay, and save extra overtime earnings if they continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious but interested. I want the tool to work; I just do not want people to disappear behind the efficiency figure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you test first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d replay the coat-count mistake across three stores and see whether the tool names the bad data feed. A nice answer that misses the source is not a fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask for in the talks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written floor for night coverage and paid time to learn the tool. If the company removes overtime, I need to know before I promise that money to the rent account.

say: I want **productivity gains** shared instead of hidden entry-level cuts.
I would join **workplace talks** on paid training and night coverage.
think: I see AI drafting **code and checks** faster than a new developer.
I fear a smaller crew could cut my **overtime pay**.
do: **Learn AI tracing** on the stock-error log this month.
**Join workplace talks** on staffing and on-call pay in the first year.
**Save extra overtime** only if those earnings continue.
feel: **Anxious but interested** in a useful tool and fair staffing.
S1.quote: I just do not want people to disappear behind the efficiency figure.
fieldNote: He is already a **daily user**, but the stock tracing method is new learning.
His worry is **overtime income** and junior jobs, not a dislike of AI.

steps.text: Learn AI stock-error tracing and compare results with the incident log
Join workplace group talks on staffing and on-call pay
Save additional overtime pay only if those shifts continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A team lead title would not stop full AGI from writing our inventory system. I’d ask the workplace group to demand a timetable and paid transition terms; warehouse robots around 2031 are a later change for the floor staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Almost all of my work is design, code and checking, so 2028 reaches me before the robots. Three months saved cannot carry a long search when the other developers in town are looking too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d call a workplace group meeting now and ask for written notice and paid retraining terms. I’d cancel the plan to buy a new motorbike and apply for paid warehouse systems support openings if my developer role ends after 2028; I would not leave for an unpaid idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel alarmed, even though I like change. I can move fast, but I cannot make a company create a paid vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Nia about the bike?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my partner Nia the bike can wait until we know whether my salary survives. It would take 2,000 from a cushion I may need for rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why warehouse systems support?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know how our software talks to scanners and staff, and that may be useful for a while. I would only take an offer if it pays enough to cover our share of rent and basic bills.

say: I’d tell colleagues **full AGI by 2028** threatens inventory developers, including leads.
I want **written transition terms** now; warehouse robots come later, around 2031.
think: I know my **design and code** work faces the 2028 thinking shock.
I fear **three months saved** will not last through a crowded developer search.
do: **Call a workplace group** meeting on written notice and paid retraining now.
**Cancel the motorbike purchase** to keep 2,000 in savings.
**Apply for paid support** if displaced after 2028; accept offers only if pay covers my share of rent and basic bills.
feel: **Alarmed** despite my comfort with new tools.
S2.quote: A team lead title would not stop full AGI from writing our inventory system.
fieldNote: His **daily AI comfort** does not blunt the risk to a desk-based lead role.
The **motorbike purchase** is the immediate expense he can cancel to protect rent money.

steps.text: Call a workplace group meeting on written notice and paid retraining
Cancel the planned motorbike purchase and keep 2,000 saved
Apply for paid warehouse systems support if displaced after 2028
Accept support offers only if pay covers my share of rent and basic bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say 2031 gives us time to test which inventory work customers still pay people to do. The company should publish a training budget and a plan for staff before calling any change orderly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My coding and planning would still meet full AGI in 2031, while warehouse robots would arrive around 2034. Five years gives me a chance to build savings and prove whether working with retail staff suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d request a funded rotation with our customer support team for one day each month and take it if approved. I’d also aim to save 250 monthly if overtime remains; after 2031 I’d apply for paid support lead openings only if the posts still exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious, but I could measure progress instead of guessing. A real budget would make a customer support rotation a job path rather than a favour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on that support day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d sit with the retail staff who reconcile missing stock and log the questions our software cannot answer. I would ask who funds a permanent support lead post before treating it as a fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my current job and continue the workplace talks about paid training. I would not mark the rotation on my record until I had actually done it.

say: I want a **training budget** and staff plan before the company calls a 2031 change orderly.
I think five years permits **customer tests** of what people still need.
think: I know **coding and planning** face AGI in 2031, ahead of robots around 2034.
I could build **savings and support experience** if funded work is available.
do: **Request a funded** monthly customer support rotation and attend only if approved.
**Save 250 monthly** if overtime continues, then apply for paid support leads if posts remain.
feel: **Anxious but focused** on measurable progress and actual funding.
S3.quote: A real budget would make a customer support rotation a job path rather than a favour.
fieldNote: He wants the **rotation funded** and linked to a real support post.
The **2031 deadline** affects his thinking work directly; robots reach warehouse floor tasks about three years later, around 2034.

steps.text: Attend a monthly customer support rotation only if the company funds it
Save 250 monthly if overtime pay continues
Apply for paid support lead posts if available after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade is enough time for our company and workers to bargain over the gains and test new roles. I would still be clear that full AGI reaches our screen work in 2036, before warehouse robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 37 then, with decades of working life ahead of me. If I keep earning, I could build a year of expenses and find out whether I like managing customer problems more than code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I’d keep using AI on code reviews and ask for one funded retail support shift each quarter. If those shifts are approved, I’d learn the work and save 200 a month while pay holds; if the developer role ends after 2036, I’d search for paid retail systems work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy, but not cornered. Ten years lets me test a route with real customers while I still draw a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How will you know the route is real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the support director for paid openings and what the job actually earns. I will not call a quarterly customer support visit a career until somebody offers wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the workplace group to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask it to bargain for training time that workers can use without losing pay. A company can call a course free while taking away a shift.

say: I want workers to **bargain over gains** and test new roles over the decade.
I’d tell colleagues **thinking work changes** in 2036, before warehouse robots around 2039.
think: I still face **decades of work** at 37.
I could build a **year of expenses** and test customer work if earnings hold.
do: **Keep reviewing code** with AI while asking for funded quarterly support shifts.
**Learn retail support** on approved paid shifts and save 200 monthly while pay holds.
**Search for paid work** in retail systems if my developer role ends after 2036.
feel: **Uneasy but not cornered** with time to test a paid route.
S4.quote: A company can call a course free while taking away a shift.
fieldNote: His daily **AI code review** continues, while funded retail shifts would teach new work.
He wants **wages and openings** verified before naming support a career path.

steps.text: Keep reviewing inventory code with AI while employed
Learn retail support on approved funded quarterly shifts
Save 200 monthly while developer pay holds
Search for paid retail systems work if displaced after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because nearly all my work is thinking work and three months of savings would disappear fast. Written notice, paid retraining and enough income to cover rent during a real job move would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether faster code gives workers shorter nights. I would like the company to measure that, because a tool that only makes us cover more stores has not improved my life.

headlineQuote: I will not call a quarterly customer support visit a career until somebody offers wages.
portrait: Colin is a **27-year-old lead developer** with a master’s degree and about three months of expenses saved.
He uses **AI every day** on inventory software, but still checks changes against real shop counts.
He favours **workplace bargaining** over staffing and training while testing new tools quickly.
The **2028 case** alarms him because coding and planning change before warehouse robots arrive.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his developer work before a three-month cushion supports a new paid role.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, paid retraining and rent-covering income during a real job move would help.
